name: Kerewo

new_statements.quote: Wurm 1973 p.226: "The suprasegmental systems are relatively complicated and manifest themselves in complex stress systems with rhythm patterns, and a two-tone system is present in all the languages, except apparently in Wabuda. Its functional load appears to be low in all the languages except for North-Eastern Kiwai and (Arigibi?) where it seems to be quite high." p.250: "Stress features yet to be studied in detail in North-Eastern Kiwai and the other Kiwaian languages may play a part in this." SIL Kerewo OPD p.3: "Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Tone is phonemic but its functional load is low."
new_statements.citation: Wurm, S.A. 1973. The Kiwaian language family. In K.J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea, 217-260. Pacific Linguistics C-26. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C26.217 (sec. 6.51 Phonology, p.226; sec. 6.66.4, p.250). Echoed for Kerewo specifically by [SIL PNG] n.d., Organised Phonology Data: Kerewo [KXZ], p.3.
new_statements.locator: Wurm 1973 p.226 (sec. 6.51) and p.250; SIL Kerewo OPD p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress placement is given. Kerewo, like the other Kiwaian languages, is described as having a 'complex stress system with rhythm patterns' plus a two-tone system of low functional load; Wurm says explicitly that the stress features of the Kiwaian languages have yet to be studied in detail, and the Kerewo OPD's suprasegmental section records only that tone is phonemic with low functional load.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (the 'rhythm patterns' phrase hints at alternating prominence but is not spelled out).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kerewo. Wabuda is said to lack the two-tone system; North-Eastern Kiwai (and Arigibi) have a higher tonal functional load.
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level (Kiwaian) generalisation; word vs phrase domain not specified; the OPD statement is for Kerewo [kxz] but is compiled from Wurm 1973 and wordlists, not new fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Wurm 1973 p.226) is a family-level generalisation over all Kiwaian languages (kiwa1251), which explicitly include Kerewo (Wurm cites Kerewo forms and features on the same page); Wurm 1971 treats 'Kerewo (Goari)' as a language with Morigi/Gama River dialects forming a transition to Bamu Kiwai. The SIL OPD is for Kerewo [kxz] = kere1286 under the names Kerewa, Kerewa-Goari, Baia, Goaribari, Wadi (Kikori, Gulf Province) and is compiled from Wurm 1973 and the Franklin & Z'graggen 1975 wordlists rather than from new fieldwork.

sources.note: p.226 sec. 6.51 (all Kiwaian languages, Kerewo explicitly included, e.g. 'the very rare presence of -nd- in Kerewo'): 'complex stress systems with rhythm patterns, and a two-tone system is present in all the languages, except apparently in Wabuda. Its functional load appears to be low...'. p.250: 'Stress features yet to be studied in detail in North-Eastern Kiwai and the other Kiwaian languages'. Kerewo forms cited (puru?o 'mouth', gagari 'bow') carry no stress marks. No statement of stress position.

sources.citation: Wurm, S.A. 1975. The Trans-Fly (sub-phylum-level) stock. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study vol. 1, 323-344. Pacific Linguistics C-38. DOI 10.15144/PL-C38.323.
sources.note: Stock-level: 'they all share a suprasegmental system which manifests itself in a complex stress system with rhythm principles, and in addition, the languages of the Kiwaian and Eastern Trans-Fly Families seem to possess a two-tone system with usually low to very low functional load'; Kiwaian sketch (Island Kiwai based) repeats it. No position; Kerewo only named in the family list.

sources.citation: Wurm, S.A. 1971. Notes on the linguistic situation in the Trans-Fly area. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 14, 115-172. Pacific Linguistics A-28. DOI 10.15144/PL-A28.115.
sources.note: Kerewo (Goari) paragraph: about 1,400 speakers, Omati mouth to Bevan Sound and Kikori; published materials Ray 1923, Capell 1962, Wurm 1951 notes; 'Rev. B. Butcher produced a manuscript grammar of Kerewo'; Franklin collected Turama-Kerewo materials 1971; Kerewo characterised by glottal-stop replacement/loss of intervocalic consonants. Family phonology paragraph repeats 'complex stress system... two-tone system' (per the sout2949 audit). No Kerewo stress-position statement.

sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': only 'Tone is phonemic but its functional load is low.' Nothing on stress placement; no stress marks anywhere (apostrophes = glottal stop). 'Linguistic work done by' / 'Data checked by' left blank; bibliography = Wurm 1973 and Franklin & Z'graggen 1975, so it is compiled from published data. fetched sources via Wayback (capture 20240617054321) because sil.org's direct PDF link is Cloudflare-403 from our machine.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1923. The languages of the Western Division of Papua. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 53: 332-360.
sources.note: Kerewa listed (p.335) as 'Village on Goaribari Island' in the Kiwai group with a comparative vocabulary; 'Note on Orthography' (p.336) only adopts Annual Report spelling; grammar notes (pp.337ff) treat Kiwai/Wabuda etc. No accent or stress statement for any language.
No phonology at all; notes Gospels published in the Goaribari dialect in 1941; cites only Ethnologue.
